key_terms: One unit of executor concurrency in which a task can run. Adding slots helps only if the plan exposes enough parallel work.
The chain of dependent stages that bounds a query's completion time, so speeding up any work off this path does not shorten the query.
A controlled comparison, such as one versus two task slots on the same fixture, that records versions, source identity, partitions, CPU and memory with each timing.
Returning a result to the client only when its size is known to be small, since collection moves every result row into one process.

worked_examples.title: Compare one and two task slots on a fixed host
worked_examples.code:
cd work/ballista
bash run.sh one-slot
bash run.sh check
bash run.sh two-slots
bash run.sh check
bash run.sh evidence
worked_examples.interpretation: Each check writes a receipt with elapsed_seconds and the same source_sha256, so the two runs can be compared on identical input. Expect the rows to match exactly and the timings to differ by an amount that is noisy at this tiny scale. The container CPU and memory limits do not change between runs, so two slots compete for the same cores; a lack of speedup is evidence about the critical path, not a broken cluster.

worked_examples.title: Limit rows and bytes before collecting
worked_examples.interpretation: This fragment from the project client puts the LIMIT in the query so executors stop early and the client receives at most three rows, then enforces a byte budget on what it will print. Collecting a full table and slicing in Python would move every row through the scheduler first. Treat a row limit and a byte limit as separate controls, since three rows with large text values can still exceed a safe response size.

evidence: Project-only actual product commands with independent fixture oracles. Source preparation, native runtime observations and restart evidence are recorded separately in the workshop qualification ledger.
